taxes.base: Income of individuals and net profit of companies (the federal tax is levied alongside the cantonal and communal taxes on the same assessment).

rate.headline: Individuals up to 11.5%; companies 8.5% of profit
details: Individuals: progressive scale topping out at 11.5% (Art. 36 DBG); companies: a flat 8.5% of net profit (Art. 68 DBG).
From 2026 a federal supplementary tax applies to large multinationals under the OECD minimum tax; its revenue is expected at about CHF 1.6 billion.

instruments.explanation: The Confederation’s largest tax, collected by the cantons on its behalf: the cantons keep 21.2% of the proceeds. Revenue was CHF 27.8 billion in 2023 and CHF 32.1 billion in 2025.
exceptions: There is no federal tax on wealth, capital gains of private individuals on securities, or inheritance.

taxes.base: Supplies of goods and services in Switzerland and imports.
taxes.payer: Consumers; businesses charge it and deduct input tax.

rate.headline: 8.1% standard; 2.6% reduced; 3.8% accommodation
details: Rates since 1 January 2024: 8.1%, 2.6% on food, books and medicines and 3.8% for hotel accommodation (Art. 25 MWSTG). The increase of 0.4 points from 2024 finances the old-age pension.

instruments.explanation: One of the lowest VAT rates in Europe. The Constitution caps the rate, so any increase needs a popular vote. Part of the proceeds is earmarked for the old-age pension scheme (AHV).
exceptions: Health care, education, culture and insurance are exempt.

taxes.base: Interest and dividends from Swiss sources, and lottery winnings.
taxes.payer: The payer deducts it; residents who declare the income get it back.

rate.headline: 35% at source
details: 35% of interest, dividends and lottery winnings (Art. 13 VStG); refunded in full to persons who declare the income correctly.

instruments.explanation: A security tax: it encourages taxpayers to declare their capital income. The yield is volatile because it depends on refunds.

taxes.base: Petrol, diesel, heating oil and natural gas used as fuel, by volume.
taxes.payer: Importers and refineries; passed on at the pump.

rate.headline: About CHF 0.73 per litre petrol, CHF 0.76 diesel
details: Petrol CHF 0.7312 and diesel CHF 0.7587 per litre including the CHF 0.30 surcharge, which is earmarked for road and air transport.

instruments.explanation: Earmarked in large part: the surcharge and half of the basic tax fund roads and air traffic.
exceptions: Refunds for agriculture, public transport and professional users of off-road machinery.

taxes.base: Transfers of Swiss and foreign securities through Swiss dealers, and certain insurance premiums.
taxes.payer: The parties to the transaction; the dealer remits it.

rate.headline: 0.15% Swiss securities; 0.3% foreign
details: The issuance stamp duty on equity was abolished from 1 January 2022; the securities transfer stamp duty remains.

instruments.explanation: A tax on financial transactions, mostly the securities transfer stamp duty.

taxes.base: Cigarettes and other tobacco products.
taxes.payer: Manufacturers and importers; passed on in the price.

rate.headline: Per piece plus a share of the retail price
details: Part of the tax is earmarked for the old-age pension scheme (AHV).

instruments.explanation: Excise on tobacco, with part of the proceeds going to the AHV.

taxes.base: Distance driven by heavy goods vehicles on Swiss roads, by weight and emission class.

rate.headline: Per tonne-kilometre by emission class
details: Charged per tonne-kilometre; lower for cleaner vehicles. Two thirds of the proceeds go to the Confederation, one third to the cantons.

instruments.explanation: A distance-based charge on lorries that replaced a flat road tax in 2001; earmarked for transport.

taxes.base: Imports, mainly agricultural goods, by weight.

rate.headline: Per 100 kg gross weight
details: Customs duties on industrial goods were abolished from 1 January 2024; those on agricultural goods remain.

instruments.explanation: Switzerland charges duty by the weight of the goods, not their value, and now only on agricultural products.

names.official: Übrige Fiskaleinnahmen (Automobilsteuer, Biersteuer, Spielbankenabgabe, Lenkungsabgaben u. a.)

taxes.base: Imported and new cars, beer, casino gaming, steering levies such as the CO₂ levy and others.

rate.headline: Different rate for each tax
details: Reported by the Federal Finance Administration as one line.

instruments.explanation: The remaining federal tax revenue after the named taxes.

taxes.base: Gross earnings, with no ceiling on contributions (the pension itself is capped).
taxes.payer: Employees and employers in equal halves; the self-employed and non-employed pay on a sliding scale.

rate.headline: 8.7% (4.35% each) of earnings
details: Contributions of 8.7% in total for AHV; further percentages are added for the IV, EO and ALV. A 13th monthly pension, approved by popular vote in March 2024, is first paid in December 2026.

instruments.explanation: The first pillar of the pension system, a pay-as-you-go scheme. VAT, the tobacco tax and the federal budget also contribute to it.

taxes.base: Gross earnings.
taxes.payer: Employees and employers in equal halves.

instruments.explanation: Pays disability pensions and rehabilitation.

taxes.base: Gross earnings.
taxes.payer: Employees and employers in equal halves.

instruments.explanation: Pays an allowance to people on military or civil service, and maternity and paternity leave.

taxes.base: Gross earnings up to a ceiling.
taxes.payer: Employees and employers in equal halves.

rate.headline: 2.2% (1.1% each) up to the ceiling
details: Charged on earnings up to a ceiling of CHF 148,200 a year.

instruments.explanation: Pays unemployment benefit and job-placement measures.

taxes.base: Income of residents, assessed together with the federal and communal taxes.

rate.headline: Each canton sets its own scale
details: Each canton fixes its own tax scale, allowances and, with the communes, the multiple that applies; the Tax Harmonisation Act fixes only the structure.

instruments.explanation: The cantons’ biggest tax, and the main way that Swiss tax competition works: a person’s total tax depends strongly on the canton and commune of residence.

names.official: Kantonale Gewinn- und Kapitalsteuer der juristischen Personen

taxes.base: Net profit and equity of companies.

rate.headline: Set by each canton
details: Each canton sets the profit and capital tax rates; the combined burden with the federal tax differs widely between cantons.

instruments.explanation: Cantons compete for companies; the 2020 tax reform (STAF) ended special regimes for holding companies and cantons cut their rates.

taxes.base: Net wealth of individuals (assets minus debts), including real estate and securities.

rate.headline: Set by each canton; low rates on the base
details: All cantons levy a net wealth tax at low rates; there is no federal wealth tax.

instruments.explanation: Switzerland is one of the few OECD countries that taxes net wealth every year, and it raises more than the inheritance and gift taxes.

taxes.base: Inheritances and gifts.

rate.headline: Set by each canton
details: Almost all cantons exempt spouses and direct descendants, and some (for example Schwyz) levy no such tax at all.

instruments.explanation: Left to the cantons; there is no federal inheritance tax.
exceptions: Spouses and children are exempt in nearly every canton.

names.official: Kantonale Motorfahrzeugsteuern und Abgaben auf der Benutzung von Gütern

taxes.base: Ownership and use of vehicles, by weight, engine power or emissions.

instruments.explanation: Annual vehicle taxes that each canton levies on its own scale.

names.official: Übrige kantonale Einkommenssteuern (nicht auf natürliche und juristische Personen aufteilbar)

taxes.base: Taxes on income and gains that the OECD cannot split between individuals and companies.

instruments.explanation: The OECD books CHF 1,942 million of cantonal income taxes as unallocated between individuals and companies.

taxes.base: Immovable property, transactions, specific goods and services and other cantonal taxes.

instruments.explanation: The rest of the cantons’ tax revenue: recurrent taxes on immovable property (CHF 450 million), other recurrent property taxes (937), financial and capital transactions (234), specific goods and services (667), other taxes (449) and an unallocated remainder.

taxes.base: The same assessed income as the cantonal tax; the commune applies its own multiple to the cantonal tax.

rate.headline: Cantonal tax × the commune’s multiple
details: The commune sets a multiple (Steuerfuss) each year on the cantonal "simple tax"; multiples vary by commune.

instruments.explanation: Swiss communes raise a large part of their own revenue from this tax, which makes them far less dependent on grants than local governments in most countries.

names.official: Kommunale Gewinn- und Kapitalsteuer der juristischen Personen

taxes.base: The cantonal profit and capital tax base, taxed again at the commune’s multiple.

instruments.explanation: In most cantons the communes levy a multiple of the cantonal company tax as well.

taxes.base: The cantonal net wealth base, taxed at the commune’s multiple.

instruments.explanation: Communes add their multiple to the cantonal wealth tax.

taxes.base: Immovable property tax, other recurrent property taxes, transactions, and income taxes not split between individuals and companies.

instruments.explanation: The rest of the communes’ tax revenue: unallocated income taxes (CHF 1,748 million), immovable property (984), other recurrent property taxes (309), transactions and inheritance (185), goods and services (271), other (546).
